distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer source-level disease leaf for bloodstream infection arising from a central venous catheter, implanted port, PICC, tunneled dialysis catheter, or comparable central intravascular access. Catheter type, organism, dialysis, TPN, oncology, ICU status, septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, and septic shock are context axes, treatment modifiers, event hazards, or related leaves rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: This leaf represents the catheter/source geometry of bloodstream infection. Organism-level bacteremia or candidemia leaves may later be superposed when post-workup pathogen identity is intentionally modeled; line-tip culture, differential time-to-positivity, susceptibility, final source adjudication, and treatment response remain confirmatory or treatment-context evidence for presentation-only tests.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation-only ranking should use central-line presence, catheter/source context, exit-site or tunnel signs when observed, fever or blunted fever, chills, vitals, systemic inflammation, CBC, CRP/PCT/lactate/renal labs, and observed endovascular complications. Blood culture species, susceptibility, DTTP, catheter-tip culture, and final source adjudication are non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly includes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Microbial adherence and biofilm formation on catheter hub, lumen, port reservoir, external surface, fibrin sheath, thrombus, or catheter tip creates a protected intravascular nidus.

Organisms enter blood through contaminated catheter hub, infusate, parenteral nutrition, catheter tract, exit-site/tunnel infection, hematogenous seeding of a catheter, or manipulation of central access.
Density and persistence of viable bacteria or fungi in blood from a central-line nidus; drives culture positivity, rigors, inflammatory response, persistence, metastatic seeding, and mortality risk.

Complement, neutrophil, monocyte, cytokine, and acute-phase response to bloodstream infection; fever and leukocytosis may be blunted in older, renal, neutropenic, steroid-treated, or immunocompromised hosts.

Long catheter dwell time, hemodialysis access, TPN, home infusion, ICU care, malignancy, neutropenia, transplant, steroids, diabetes, renal failure, skin breakdown, and frequent line manipulation increase colonization, impaired clearance, and relapse.
Ongoing seeding from a retained infected catheter, port, thrombus, fibrin sheath, catheter tunnel, or incompletely controlled intravascular focus despite antimicrobial exposure.

Catheter biofilm, infected fibrin sheath, septic thrombus, right atrial catheter-tip lesion, valve/device seeding, and embolization produce septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis hazard, pulmonary embolic lesions, and persistence.

Distributive shock, endothelial leak, hypoperfusion, AKI, respiratory failure or ARDS, encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia, liver injury, and DIC-like coagulopathy from bloodstream infection and vulnerable host reserve.

Empiric regimen mismatch, resistant gram-positive/gram-negative/fungal organism, underdosing in renal replacement therapy, allergy constraints, weak antifungal coverage, or delayed therapy prolongs bloodstream burden.

Hemodialysis access is a recurring CLABSI context.
TPN and home infusion increase hub manipulation and fungal/biofilm risk.
Cancer therapy, transplant drugs, biologics, and steroids impair clearance.
Recent broad antibiotics select resistant bacteria and Candida.
Long dwell time, manipulation, TPN, dialysis, and hospital exposure increase biofilm colonization.
Colonized catheter surfaces and hubs seed organisms into blood.
Extraluminal or tunnel infection can manifest as erythema, swelling, tenderness, or drainage.
Infection may track along a tunneled catheter even if bacteremia is the main presentation.
Observed central access plus compatible systemic illness raises catheter-source probability.
Biofilm and catheter-tip or hub colonization raise infected-catheter probability.
Line-associated entry generates bloodstream burden.
A retained infected line, sheath, or thrombus continues seeding blood.
Viable bloodstream burden raises blood culture positivity; organism identity remains confirmatory for presentation-only ranking.
Ongoing burden produces persistent or recurrent bacteremia/fungemia.
Circulating organisms trigger innate inflammation.
Pyrogenic cytokines cause fever, though response may be blunted.
Fever history is common in line-associated bacteremia or fungemia.
Bloodstream infection often causes chills or rigors, sometimes during dialysis or infusion.
Fever, inflammation, hypovolemia, and sepsis physiology increase heart rate.
Fever, acidosis, hypoxemia, or shock increase respiratory rate.
Leukocytosis is common, but severe immunosuppression or overwhelming sepsis may blunt the count.
Neutrophilic response tracks invasive bacterial inflammation when marrow reserve is intact.
Relative neutrophilia is common in bacterial CLABSI.
CRP rises in catheter-related bloodstream infection.
PCT can rise in bacterial bloodstream infection and septic organ dysfunction, but may be lower in some fungal or low-burden cases.
Systemic inflammation produces malaise and fatigue.
Distributive shock lowers systolic pressure.
Septic vasodilation and capillary leak lower MAP.
Hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate.
AKI, shock, nephrotoxic therapy, or renal background can raise creatinine.
AKI, catabolic stress, dehydration, or dialysis context affects BUN.
Sepsis, DIC, critical illness, or marrow disease may lower platelets.
ARDS, septic emboli, pneumonia, fluid overload, or shock may lower oxygenation.
Severe CLABSI sepsis can worsen oxygenation ratio.
Sepsis encephalopathy, shock, hypoxemia, or metabolic injury alters mental status.
Shock liver, inflammation, or critical illness can raise AST.
Shock liver or drug toxicity can raise ALT.
Hypotension, lactate elevation, and vasopressor need represent shock pathway.
Shock, renal background, and nephrotoxic treatment raise AKI hazard.
Sepsis, fluid resuscitation, pneumonia, or septic emboli can trigger ARDS.
Severe bloodstream infection can produce DIC-like coagulopathy.
Biofilm on catheter, fibrin sheath, or thrombus can seed endovascular complications.
Infected catheter thrombus can appear as septic thrombophlebitis.
Catheter thrombus and persistent bacteremia raise thrombophlebitis hazard.
Persistent catheter-associated bloodstream infection can seed valves or cardiac devices.
Septic thrombus or endocarditis can embolize.
Retained line, port, sheath, or thrombus requires removal, exchange, lock strategy, drainage, or thrombectomy depending context.
Before removal or adequate control, source-control adequacy is low.
Mismatch, resistance, dosing, or allergy lowers active antibacterial coverage.
Fungal CLABSI requires antifungal-active context; antibacterial therapy alone does not cover it.
Inactive therapy prolongs bacteremia or fungemia.
Shock, AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, and multiorgan failure drive early mortality.
Uncontrolled line or endovascular nidus prolongs burden and worsens survival.
Delayed or inactive treatment increases persistence, organ failure, and death risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing oxygen_saturation pathway.

axes.shape_free_text: Central venous catheter, implanted port, PICC, tunneled dialysis catheter, or comparable central intravascular access present.
Probability that the central line, port, catheter hub, catheter tip, or catheter-associated thrombus is the bloodstream source.
Probability that the catheter or port itself is infected or colonized enough to sustain bloodstream infection.
Erythema, swelling, tenderness, purulence, drainage, or cellulitis at the catheter exit site or port pocket.
Induration, pain, erythema, drainage, or abscess along a tunneled catheter tract or port pocket.
Hemodialysis catheter, fistula, graft, or dialysis access context.
Current or recent parenteral nutrition through central venous access, including home TPN.
Recent broad-spectrum antibacterial or antifungal exposure selecting resistant bacteria or fungi.
Intensity of chemotherapy, transplant immunosuppression, biologics, chronic steroids, or other iatrogenic immune suppression.
Probability that blood cultures are positive for a bloodstream infection; organism identity remains confirmatory/non-ranking unless post-workup mode is used.
Hours by which catheter-drawn culture becomes positive before peripheral culture. This is confirmatory/source-adjudication evidence, not ordinary presentation-only evidence.
Probability that removed catheter tip or port culture grows the same organism. This is confirmatory/source-control evidence, not ordinary presentation-only evidence.
Duration of persistent or recurrent positive blood cultures from line-associated bloodstream infection.
Measured body temperature; can be high, low, or blunted depending host reserve.
Reported fever, relapsing fever, or fever during infusion or dialysis.
Chills or rigors accompanying bloodstream infection, including infusion- or dialysis-associated episodes.
Heart rate; tachycardia tracks fever, pain, shock, and sepsis physiology.
Respiratory rate; rises with fever, acidosis, hypoxemia, shock, or respiratory failure.
Systolic blood pressure; may fall with CLABSI septic shock.
Mean arterial pressure; lower values indicate distributive shock unless supported.
Pulse oxygen saturation; can fall with ARDS, septic emboli, pneumonia, fluid overload, or shock.

Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement: 0 room air, 1 low-flow nasal cannula, 2 mask or higher low-flow support, 3 high-flow nasal cannula, 4 noninvasive ventilation, 5 invasive ventilation or extracorporeal support.
PaO2/FiO2 ratio; lower values reflect hypoxemic respiratory failure or ARDS in severe sepsis.
Confusion, reduced consciousness, sepsis encephalopathy, or shock-related altered mental status.
Malaise, fatigue, poor energy, or nonspecific systemic illness.
Nausea or vomiting from systemic infection, antibiotics, or underlying source context; not specific for CLABSI.
Diarrhea from systemic illness, antibiotic exposure, enteral disease context, or C. difficile risk; not specific for CLABSI.
White blood cell count; often elevated but can be normal or low in immunosuppressed hosts.
Absolute neutrophil count; rises with intact myeloid response and falls with marrow suppression or neutropenia.
Neutrophil percentage on differential.
Hemoglobin; reflects anemia, chronic disease, renal failure, bleeding, or critical illness background.
Platelet count; may fall with sepsis, DIC, marrow disease, dialysis, or critical illness.
C-reactive protein, elevated in systemic inflammation and deep catheter-source infection.
Procalcitonin; often rises with bacterial bloodstream infection and shock, lower or variable in fungal or low-burden cases.
Serum lactate; rises with shock and tissue hypoperfusion.
Serum creatinine; affected by CKD, dialysis, AKI, shock, and nephrotoxic therapy.
Blood urea nitrogen; affected by renal failure, dialysis, dehydration, and catabolic stress.
Serum albumin; low values reflect malnutrition, inflammation, chronic disease, or capillary leak.
AST; can rise with shock liver, critical illness, or drug toxicity.
ALT; can rise with shock liver, critical illness, or drug toxicity.
Total bilirubin; can rise with shock liver, cholestasis, hemolysis, or critical illness.
Observed infected venous thrombus, catheter-tip thrombus, or septic thrombophlebitis associated with central access.
Daily hazard of developing clinically important septic thrombophlebitis from line-associated infection.
Daily hazard of valve or cardiac-device infective endocarditis during catheter-associated bloodstream infection.
Daily hazard of septic emboli from infected catheter thrombus or endocarditis.
Daily hazard of septic shock or circulatory collapse.
Daily hazard of AKI from sepsis, shock, renal background, nephrotoxic drugs, or contrast exposure.
Daily hazard of ARDS or severe inflammatory respiratory failure.
Daily hazard of DIC-like coagulopathy in severe bloodstream infection.
Daily hazard of clinically major bleeding from thrombocytopenia, DIC, anticoagulation, line procedures, thrombectomy, or critical illness.
Daily hazard of bleeding attributable to catheter removal, exchange, port removal, thrombectomy, drainage, or related source-control procedures.
Need for catheter removal, catheter exchange, port removal, drainage, thrombectomy, endovascular focus control, or line-lock salvage strategy.
Adequacy of achieved line/device removal, exchange, lock sterilization, sheath/thrombus removal, or other source control.
Probability that current antibacterial therapy has activity and adequate exposure against the responsible bacterial bloodstream pathogen.
Probability that current systemic antifungal therapy has activity against a fungal central-line bloodstream pathogen.
Need to adapt antimicrobial dose or monitoring for CKD, AKI, hemodialysis, CRRT, or renal toxicity risk.
Severe beta-lactam allergy or immediate hypersensitivity limiting empiric or directed beta-lactam therapy.

Lifespan outcome hazard for central line-associated bloodstream infection; driven by shock, organ failure, persistent bloodstream burden, resistant or fungal pathogen context, inadequate source control, thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, and host vulnerability.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia move together beyond mechanism-gated mean effects.
Inflammatory markers partially covary, though WBC may be blunted by host context.
Line removal or adequate source control shortens persistent bacteremia/fungemia.

Catheter-source infection can seed thrombus or fibrin sheath.
Active antimicrobial exposure shortens persistence when source control is adequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removal or exchange has greatest effect when the line is the nidus.
Procedural source control only helps when a controllable nidus exists.
Complete device/nidus control shortens persistence.

Renal failure and dialysis alter dosing.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Dwell time and manipulation promote biofilm.
Dialysis catheters are high-risk line sources.
Renal labs must be interpreted against CKD/dialysis background.
TPN and home access manipulation raise CLABSI risk.
TPN raises fungal bloodstream infection plausibility.
Local findings are direct source-context evidence.

supportive_care: Obtain paired peripheral and catheter-drawn blood cultures before antimicrobials when feasible, but do not delay therapy in unstable sepsis.

Treat organism species, susceptibility, catheter-tip culture, differential time-to-positivity, and final source adjudication as confirmatory or treatment-context evidence unless the workflow explicitly tests post-workup diagnosis.
Inspect the exit site, tunnel, and port pocket; evaluate line necessity, dwell time, hub manipulation, TPN/home infusion, hemodialysis access, and other source risks.
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance and reassess persistent or recurrent bloodstream infection.
Reassess source control repeatedly: line removal, exchange, port removal, lock therapy only when salvage is appropriate, drainage, thrombectomy, or endovascular intervention according to context.
Search for complications when bacteremia or fungemia persists: septic thrombophlebitis, retained fibrin sheath, endocarditis, septic emboli, metastatic foci, AKI, ARDS, and DIC-like coagulopathy.
Adjust antimicrobial choice and dosing for renal failure, dialysis, CRRT, allergy, local resistance ecology, fungal risk, and toxicity monitoring.
Provide sepsis support when needed: fluids, vasopressors, oxygen or ventilation, renal replacement therapy, lactate reassessment, and ICU monitoring.
quality_notes: No treatment-rank labels are encoded; treatment ranking should emerge from context axes and forward simulation.

Catheter type, pathogen, susceptibility, line-tip culture, DTTP, source adjudication, septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, and septic shock are context or event structures rather than disease-name qualifiers.
